newsitem.title: UK: GDR REPORT - India goes "wild" after ITC H1 figures.
newsitem.headline: GDR REPORT - India goes "wild" after ITC H1 figures.

text.p: The GDR market was shaken out of its seasonal lethargy with a frantic bout of trading on Monday, which saw the Bombay leading share index plunge almost four percent and then recover to help GDRs top Friday's close.
"Among GDRs, India was the ride of your life," said a trader. "Grasim, India Hotels, Tata, Bajaj, it was wild."
"The ITC figures came out and we concurred. The market was down 30 (points) but then rallied with ITC news to close above Friday. The buyers were coming mostly from Hong Kong."
Tobacco and hotel group ITC Ltd, in which Britain's BAT Industries plc has a 31.7 percent stake, reported a 28 percent jump in H1 net profit to 1.81 billion rupees.

It also said it would be able to pay off excise duty owed to the government by the January 1 deadline, and appointed two new independent non-executive directors to its board. Some Indian markets were closed on Monday for a religious holiday but the stock market took an initial hammering on the back of expected disappointing first half results for key companies and general pessimism on the economic outlook.
Bombay's benchmark index plunged 109.45 points or 3.7 percent to an early low of 2856.21. It then erased all losses to end 35.44 points up at a provisional 3001.10.
Among GDRs, smaller books added to the day's volatility in the market, traders said. They expect the market to open firmer tomorrow but volatility to die down.
Reliance (at 11.875), Hindalco (18.65), Bajaj Auto (30.6), Tata Engineering (11.25) and Indian Hotels (23.0) all moved up on the day.
The Cazenove Indian GDR Index was 1.47 points or 2.22 percent higher at 67.59. The premium for GDRs over stocks on the local market was 14.19 percent after 12.94 percent on Friday.
News from the Asia Pacific Economic Co-operation conference in Manila, where 18 APEC members were thrashing out trade issues for the region, had little impact, traders said.

In Korea, there was a subdued reaction to a move by the government to allow local firms to raise more capital and promote liquidity. Seoul ended at a new low for the year on oversupply fears and weak trading. The composite index was off 2.05 percent or 14.99 points to 716.45.
